claims.text: The coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The as-deposited multilayer has pronounced lattice distortion at its interfaces.
The as-deposited multilayer has short-range chemical order at its interfaces.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained load is governed by dislocation accumulation and interaction at chemically and structurally complex interfaces.
Severe interfacial lattice distortion enhances dislocation pile-up.
Short-range chemical order at interfaces enhances dislocation pile-up.
Interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order promote cross-interface slip.
Interface-mediated progressive plasticity can combine high strength with enhanced deformation tolerance.
Chemically heterogeneous and structurally distorted interfacial regions mediate dislocation nucleation.
Chemically heterogeneous and structurally distorted interfacial regions mediate dislocation pile-up and transfer between layers.
Under sustained loading, dislocations preferentially accumulate at distorted interfaces.
The local stress generated by dislocation pile-ups causes interface-mediated cross-slip.
The local stress generated by dislocation pile-ups promotes dynamic recovery.
Cross-slip and dynamic recovery gradually enable plastic deformation.
Reducing interfacial lattice distortion will lower the interfacial dislocation concentration.
Reducing interfacial lattice distortion will decrease the creep rate.
Unmodified multilayers will develop localized interfacial plastic strain through dislocation pile-up and cross-interface slip.
Modified interfaces with reduced lattice distortion will show less interface-localized deformation than unmodified interfaces.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate only when nanoscale layer dimensions and sufficient temperature and stress enable creep.
The independent contribution of short-range chemical order to dislocation behavior and plastic deformation is unclear.
